before.season: Jun-Oct scramble; also climbed Dec-Mar as a snow route

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with August as the single best month

July.reason: Early July can retain lingering snow on shaded sections; conditions firm up and become good by mid-to-late July as the route dries out

August.reason: Driest, clearest window on this transitional, drier-than-the-crest slope; best footing on heather and talus

October.reason: Outside the established season window; return of snow cover and shorter daylight make the long approach riskier

September.reason: Still dry and clear typically, though days shorten and early-season snow can arrive late in the month

climate.typical: Transitional climate, drier than the crest; clearest mid- to late summer.

crowds.peakTraffic: weekends in August when trail/scree is driest; occasional club scramble outings
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 10-25 parties per season - a known Mountaineers club scramble objective (rated around S3/T3) but well off the main Highway 2 corridor traffic

before.approach: From the unofficial roadside pullout on US-2 (room for roughly 2-3 cars, no permit needed but watch for posted no-parking signs) about 6-7 miles east of Stevens Pass near a WSDOT maintenance/tunnel-entrance yard, walk back (west) along the highway shoulder and cross to the north side just after the Nason Creek bridge. Immediately re-cross the active BNSF/Amtrak rail line that parallels the highway here — trains do run this corridor, so treat the crossing with real caution and don't linger on the tracks. On the far side, pick up an old logging grade, Forest Road 687, which runs roughly ESE/paralleling Nason Creek; expect standing runoff puddles/small ponds and a set of powerlines to duck under in the first 10-15 minutes. About 1 mile in, at roughly 2,700 ft, leave the road and scramble up the creek-cut bank into the timber, then climb steep, wooded, south-facing slopes on a compass bearing toward Arrowhead's north ridge — expect downed logs, brush, and loose duff underfoot, plus old blue/yellow forestry-marking blazes on some trees. Around 3,400 ft there is a short, slightly tricky section where minor rock/cliff bands force a bit of route-finding to skirt around (stay left/east of the steepest rock). Snow cover typically begins near 3,700 ft and can be firm/icy under the tree canopy even when it's soft in the open — many parties carry or wear microspikes/snowshoes above this point, especially in the Nov-Apr window this peak is most commonly climbed in. The timbered ridge is gained around 4,800 ft; from there the angle eases and the route trends more westerly through open glades and clearcut edges (some reports describe an alternate, gentler logging-road line up through the clearcuts on this stretch) to the summit rocks at 6,030 ft. Total one-way distance runs roughly 4.5-4.8 miles with about 3,300-3,550 ft of gain depending on the exact line taken; there is no maintained trail or trail number — this is an unmarked, route-finding scramble the whole way.

itinerary.cal: Most commonly climbed Dec-Apr with snow covering the brushy clearcut and loose ground; route crosses active Amtrak tracks near the trailhead, so watch for trains.

days.note: Standard South Route/North Ridge scramble done entirely in a single day from Highway 2 near Stevens Pass. Parties walk the highway shoulder and an old logging road/railroad grade to gain a clearcut, then climb steep timber to the north ridge and follow it to the open summit; descent reverses the ascent line.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble

schedule.label: Leave trailhead pullout on Hwy 2
schedule.detail: Walk the highway shoulder, cross Nason Creek and the active Amtrak tracks into the forest.

schedule.label: Reach base of clearcut (~4,200 ft)
schedule.detail: Ascend the old logging road/clearcut, working around minor cliff bands near 3,400 ft.

schedule.label: Gain the north ridge (~4,800 ft)
schedule.detail: Cross a flat bench east to pick up Arrowhead's north ridge proper.

schedule.label: Summit (6,030 ft)
schedule.detail: Final stretch traverses open glades/talus to the top; short break for views and food.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent route down the ridge and clearcut.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Descent often feels longer than the climb on tired legs even on the same tracks.

days.objective: Summit Arrowhead Mountain (6,030 ft) and return

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: roughly 6-7.5 hours round trip for about 3,300-3,550 ft of gain over 6-9 miles depending on snow conditions and exact line; no camp involved.

waypoints.name: US-2 roadside pullout at WSDOT maintenance yard
waypoints.note: Unmarked shoulder pullout on US-2 at the WSDOT maintenance yard turnoff (room for several cars); no permit required, no official trailhead signage.
waypoints.directions: Park at the unmarked shoulder pullout on US-2 by the WSDOT maintenance and tunnel-entrance yard, roughly 6 to 7 miles east of Stevens Pass. There is room for two or three cars and no permit is needed, but check for posted no-parking signs. Nothing here is signed — there is no trailhead, no trail number and no maintained tread anywhere on this route.

waypoints.name: Nason Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the highway then ford Nason Creek just past the FR 687/bridge area on the climbers' path; can run high and cold during spring snowmelt.
waypoints.directions: Walk back west along the highway shoulder and cross to the north side just past the Nason Creek bridge. Pick up the climbers' path and get across the creek; it runs high and cold during spring snowmelt.

waypoints.name: BNSF railroad grade crossing
waypoints.note: Route briefly follows the old railroad/powerline grade paralleling the creek and crosses the active BNSF Stevens Pass line (Empire Builder route) — look both ways, trains run frequently.
waypoints.directions: On the far side the route joins the old railroad and powerline grade running beside the creek, which means crossing the active BNSF Stevens Pass main line. Trains use this corridor frequently — look both ways and do not linger on the tracks.

waypoints.name: Leave grade, begin timbered ascent
waypoints.note: About 1 mile from the highway the route leaves the railroad/powerline grade and scrambles up a steep timbered bank — this is the start of the unmarked climb to the northeast ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the grade (Forest Road 687) roughly east-southeast alongside Nason Creek for about a mile, ducking under a set of powerlines and skirting standing runoff ponds in the first ten to fifteen minutes. At around 2,700 ft leave the grade and scramble up the creek-cut bank into the timber. Nothing marks the spot, so pick your line off the map rather than looking for a path.

waypoints.name: Minor cliff bands in the timber
waypoints.note: Short rock cliff bands force route-finding through the trees around 3,400 ft; stay alert for the path of least resistance to avoid getting cliffed out.
waypoints.directions: Climb steep, wooded slopes on a compass bearing, over downed logs and loose duff, with old blue and yellow forestry blazes on some trees. Around 3,400 ft short rock bands break the slope — work around them at the path of least resistance rather than pressing straight up, since the terrain here is broken enough to cliff you out.

waypoints.name: Gain the northeast shoulder/ridge
waypoints.note: Steep timber eases onto the mountain's northeast ridge here (reported 4,600-4,800 ft); turn and follow the ridge crest through heather and talus toward the summit.
waypoints.directions: The timber stays steep above the rock bands until the angle eases onto the crest somewhere between 4,600 and 4,800 ft. Snow cover usually starts near 3,700 ft and can be firm or icy under the tree canopy even when it is soft in the open, so this is where most parties put on microspikes or snowshoes.

waypoints.name: Arrowhead Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit (6,030 ft) with views of Glacier Peak, the Chiwaukum Mountains, and Jim Hill Mountain; no register commonly reported.
waypoints.directions: From the shoulder, turn and follow the crest southeast through open glades, heather and talus to the summit rocks. The angle eases here and the going is the easiest of the day, but the route stays unmarked to the top and the clearcut edges along this stretch make it easy to drift off the crest.

itinerary.cal: Core Enchantment Zone overnight permits (required for the basin camp, roughly June 15-Oct 31) are lottery/walk-up only and are among the hardest to get in Washington; plan well ahead or be ready to camp lower and day-trip the summit instead.

days.note: From the Snow Lakes trailhead (~1,300 ft), climb the long, steadily steepening Snow Lakes Trail past Nada and Snow Lakes and up into the core Enchantment basin, camping near Perfection or Inspiration Lake (~7,500 ft). A Core Enchantment Zone overnight permit is required in season and is hard to draw/walk up for.
days.title: Hike in to core Enchantment basin

days.note: A long out-and-back day-climb from camp: up past Talisman/Rune Lakes to Prusik Pass, northwest around Lorelei Lakelets and up onto Druid Plateau, then west up scree/snow to the summit block and a final friction-slab scramble. This typically takes roughly 9-9.5 hours round trip in good conditions; expect longer if snow lingers on the plateau or the summit block is wet/icy.
days.title: Climb Cannon Mountain from camp

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Depart Perfection/Inspiration Lake camp after breakfast, heading toward Talisman and Rune Lakes.

schedule.label: Reach Prusik Pass
schedule.detail: ~7,463 ft; contour northwest from here staying high (7,300-7,400 ft) past the Lorelei Lakelets.

schedule.label: Gain Druid Plateau
schedule.detail: Climb the rib to ~7,900-8,000 ft then up to the plateau at ~8,350 ft; summit comes into view.

schedule.label: Reach the summit
schedule.detail: West slopes to the summit block, then the friction-slab ramp on its south side to the top (~8,600+ ft).

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the route down through Druid Plateau and Lorelei Lakelets to Prusik Pass.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Round trip typically ~9-9.5 hours; strong parties can be faster in firm snow conditions.

days.objective: Tag the Cannon Mountain summit and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach: descend from the core basin back down the Snow Lakes Trail past Snow and Nada Lakes to the trailhead. Knees take a beating on the steep switchbacks below Snow Lakes; many parties budget extra time versus the hike in.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Break camp and return to the Snow Lakes trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A standard 3-day, 2-night trip: ~9-10.5 mile carries on the in/out days (~6,000 ft each way) bracketing a long ~9-9.5 hour, ~2,300 ft round-trip summit day from a core Enchantment basecamp; very fit parties compress the summit push and hike-out into one very long single day.

before.approach: Start at the Snow Lakes Trailhead (paved, day-use permit required, ~4 miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth). Follow the Snow Lakes Trail (#1553) as it climbs through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, passing Nada and Snow Lakes (roughly 6-7 miles in) before continuing up into the core Enchantment Lakes basin — Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun Lake, Sprite Lake, and Perfection Lake. By the time you reach Perfection Lake you have covered on the order of 8-9 miles and about 4,500 ft of gain from the trailhead, all on maintained but rocky, sometimes eroded tread with several creek crossings that can run high with snowmelt in early season. At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the climbers'/scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass (~7,463 ft) — this junction is easy to miss and is the last reliable water before the cross-country section. From Prusik Pass the route leaves all trail: contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, staying on the left (west) side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then continue north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft, turn northwest and climb steep talus/scree (snow-covered into mid-summer) up onto the Druid Plateau (~8,350 ft), where Cannon's summit block comes into view across the plateau. Cross the plateau and take the western slopes to the base of the summit block; the final ~15 ft to the true summit is a low-angle but exposed friction slab climbed via a ramp on the block's south side, with almost no positive holds — approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference here. Because the round trip from the trailhead is roughly 30+ miles with 7,300+ ft of gain, essentially all parties camp in or near the core Enchantment zone (competitive overnight permits required in season) rather than attempting it car-to-car; treat the whole cross-country section above Prusik Pass as serious route-finding terrain with no cairns or tread, frequently holding snow into July, and exposed to sun/lightning with no bail-out shelter.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered eight or nine miles and about 4,500 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the WEST side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
hazards: No cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass — serious route-finding on talus and heather
Snow frequently lingering on the cross-country section into July
An exposed, holdless friction slab for the final fifteen feet, harder to downclimb than to climb
Verglas on shaded ground into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain
No bail-out shelter: sun, lightning and afternoon storms on open high ground
Core Zone overnight permits are competitive and effectively required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS A SEPARATE OBJECT AND THE PLATEAU IS NOT THE TOP. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct BLOCK that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

SO THE TEST IS: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the WESTERN slopes to the foot of the block.

WHICH SIDE OF THE BLOCK, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS IN CLOUD: the way up is a RAMP on the block's SOUTH side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

WHAT THE RIGHT GROUND FEELS LIKE: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

STAGING CHECK BELOW THE PLATEAU: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their WEST side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
approach_variants.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain
An exposed holdless friction ramp on the summit block
Snow and verglas on shaded ground into July
No published timing for this variant — plan conservatively
No bail-out shelter on the high ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH APPROACHES CONVERGE ON THE DRUID PLATEAU, SO THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS NOT. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are NOT on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

WHAT STILL HOLDS: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its WESTERN slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its SOUTH side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

THE NORTH-SIDE-SPECIFIC WARNING: the ground below the basin has CLIFF BANDS in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

AND A ROUTE-CHOICE NOTE: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard approach: Snow Lakes Trail #1553 (~4.2 mi up Icicle Creek Rd from US-2 in Leavenworth) into the Enchantment Lakes basin, then via Perfection Lake to Prusik Pass, traverse NW to the Druid Plateau, then to the summit block (~9 mi, ~4,500 ft gain one-way).

before.itinerary: Feasible as a very long single day done as a loop: ascend the NE Ridge from the Eightmile Trailhead parking area, then descend via Prusik Pass, the Upper Enchantments, and Aasgard Pass to the Stuart Lake Trailhead -- about 15 miles with sustained class 3 scrambling and heavy bushwhacking. Best attempted only by strong, experienced parties, with a car shuttle or road connection arranged between the two trailheads.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile trailhead and the burned slopes to the northeast ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road about eight miles, then turn left onto the signed gravel Eightmile Road, cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large lot at the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required. This route starts at the Eightmile trailhead itself, not at the Stuart Lake trailhead further up the same road system. The route climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to gain the ridge crest, then follows and traverses beneath the crest, and finishes with a talus gully and a short scramble to the summit block. It is described as an ascent route only. Most parties come down the other side of the mountain instead — Prusik Pass, the Upper Enchantment basin, down Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the Stuart Lake trailhead — which makes this a demanding roughly fifteen-mile loop with sustained Class 3 and bushwhacking, at least twelve hours car to car, and two different trailheads. Plan the car shuttle before you start walking.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, once the snow is off the ridge and out of the ground around Coney Lake
hazards: Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no trail on the lower half
A third of a mile of loose traversing below a band of unclimbable towers — the crux of the route
Sustained Class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking over a roughly fifteen-mile day
Descent is over the summit to a DIFFERENT trailhead: a car shuttle or a long road walk
At least twelve hours car to car, so an early start is not optional
Snow lingering around Coney Lake and on the ridge in early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOWERS ARE THE MARKER, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS TO GO UNDER THEM. The identifying feature of this ridge is a band of towers on the crest that CANNOT be climbed directly, and the route's answer to them is a loose traverse of about a third of a mile BELOW the crest. That traverse is the route's signature and its worst ground.

SO THE TEST WHEN YOU GAIN THE CREST IS: keep going until the crest stops being walkable. When rock towers block the ridge in front of you, do not look for a way over them — drop onto the flank and traverse beneath. A party that finds itself scrambling technical rock on the crest has missed the traverse.

AND THE ARRIVAL TEST AT THE OTHER END: the traverse ends at a TALUS GULLY. Talus, after loose sidehill traversing, is the cue that the towers are behind you. From the top of that gully it is a short scramble to the summit block.

WHAT GOING TOO LOW LOOKS LIKE: the traverse is beneath the crest, not down in the basin. If you have lost enough height that the towers are well above you and you are on continuous scree, you will have to regain it — this is the most common way the traverse costs more than the third of a mile it looks like on a map.

BEFORE ANY OF THAT — THE LOWER HALF IS THE REAL PROBLEM. Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no path, and this route is best done in mid to late summer once the snow is gone from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. Snow on the lower slopes turns an unpleasant ascent into a serious one.

AND THE DIRECTIONAL WARNING: this is an ascent-only line. Do not plan to reverse it. The descent is over the top and down the far side of the mountain to a different trailhead.

before.beta: This is one of the two main routes on Cannon Mountain and is 'only advised as an ascent route' -- most parties descend via the standard Prusik Pass/Druid Plateau line instead of reversing it. It's best done in mid-to-late summer once snow has melted from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. The route starts at the Eightmile Trailhead, climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to the ridge crest, then follows and traverses below the crest -- including a notorious 0.3-mile loose traverse below a band of towers that can't be climbed directly -- before a talus gully and short final scramble to the summit block.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required for trailhead parking
access.permit: No overnight permit needed for a single-day ascent-only trip from the Eightmile Trailhead; an Enchantment Permit Area lottery permit is required only if descending through and camping in the core zone as part of the loop option
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (Alpine Lakes Wilderness / Enchantment Permit Area)

road.name: Icicle Road / Forest Road 7600, Eightmile Road spur (Eightmile Trailhead)
road.driveNote: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (FR 7600) about 8 miles, turn left onto the signed, gravel Eightmile Road, cross Icicle Creek, and climb about 1,100 ft to the large parking area at the road's end, passing the Eightmile Creek Trailhead on the way. Northwest Forest Pass required.

waypoints.name: Cannon Mountain summit (NE Ridge route point)
